claims.text: The target phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloys exhibit marginal glass formation and modest amorphous-state thermal stability.
Adding a secondary alloying element at a concentration of a few atomic percent increases the system's mixing entropy.
Low-concentration secondary-element microalloying improves glass-forming ability in phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloys.
Low-concentration secondary-element microalloying enhances the thermal stability of the resulting amorphous state.
The expected improvement applies when modified and baseline alloys are processed at comparable cooling rates.
The secondary-element concentration must be low enough to avoid phase separation or crystalline intermetallic formation.
Secondary-element microalloying produces a more uniform atomic-size distribution.
A more uniform atomic-size distribution minimizes local lattice distortions.
Microalloying promotes a more homogeneous liquid structure before vitrification.
Minimal-content or high-entropy microalloying lowers liquid fragility.
The proposed microalloying intervention lowers liquid fragility specifically in phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloys.
Lower liquid fragility reduces the critical cooling rate required for glass formation.
A lower critical cooling rate is evidence of reduced liquid fragility.
The proposed microalloying intervention delays crystallization during heating.
The intervention increases the temperature interval between the glass transition and crystallization onset relative to an unmodified alloy.
Excessive secondary-element concentration may make the intervention ineffective or detrimental.
A secondary element with excessively dissimilar atomic size or bonding characteristics may cause phase separation.
Unfavorable interaction between the secondary element and phosphorus may negate the intervention.
